title: FitTech Apparel: segment margin analysis and the decision to drop a division
participant_role: Director of financial planning at FitTech Apparel advising on whether to eliminate the Smart Shoes division
judge_role: Chief executive officer (CEO) of FitTech Apparel, who plans to drop the Smart Shoes division because it shows a net loss

difficulty.rationale: Segment margin and drop decision; State-level math.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of director of financial planning for FITTECH APPAREL, a sports apparel and equipment company. The chief executive officer (CEO) (judge) has asked you to advise on whether to eliminate an underperforming product division.

FITTECH APPAREL operates three divisions. The Smart Shoes division has been struggling, and the CEO (judge) recently reviewed a divisional income statement showing that Smart Shoes had a net loss of $25,000 last year. The CEO (judge) intends to drop the division, expecting overall company profit to rise by $25,000.

You have gathered the underlying data for the Smart Shoes division: sales revenue of $300,000; variable expenses of $200,000; traceable fixed costs (dedicated supervisors and advertising for the shoe line only) of $60,000; and common allocated fixed costs (a share of corporate headquarters rent and of the CEO's salary) of $65,000.

[Smart Shoes division data: see exhibits]

You must:
- Distinguish between traceable fixed costs and common allocated fixed costs
- Calculate the contribution margin and the segment margin for the Smart Shoes division
- Determine the actual effect on the company's overall net income if the division is dropped
- Advise the CEO on whether the division should be eliminated, giving both financial and qualitative reasons

You will present the information to the CEO (judge) in a role-play to take place in the CEO's office. The CEO (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the CEO's (judge's) questions, the CEO (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: If we shouldn't use net loss to evaluate the Smart Shoes division manager, what should we use?
Is there any situation where dropping Smart Shoes would be the right decision?

solution.overview: A strong answer separates traceable fixed costs (avoidable if the division closes) from common allocated costs (which stay), computes a contribution margin of $100,000 and a positive segment margin of $40,000, and shows that dropping Smart Shoes would lower company net income by $40,000, not raise it by $25,000. The presenter recommends keeping the division, adds qualitative reasons, and suggests ways to improve its margin.

answer: Traceable fixed costs exist only because the segment exists (shoe supervisors, shoe advertising): they disappear if Smart Shoes closes
Common fixed costs support the whole company (headquarters rent, CEO salary): they stay if Smart Shoes closes
The $65,000 is an allocation, so closing the division just shifts it to the other two divisions
Only avoidable (differential) costs matter for the drop decision
Contribution margin: 300,000 minus 200,000 = $100,000
Segment margin: 100,000 minus 60,000 traceable = $40,000
Smart Shoes contributes $40,000 a year toward the company's common costs and profit
The $25,000 net loss appears only after subtracting the $65,000 allocation
Revenue lost $300,000; variable costs saved $200,000; traceable fixed costs saved $60,000
Net effect: 300,000 minus 200,000 minus 60,000 = $40,000 of lost income
The $65,000 of common costs remains and is charged to the other divisions
Company net income falls by $40,000; the CEO's expected $25,000 gain does not happen
Keep Smart Shoes: it covers all of its own costs and adds $40,000 to company profit
Improve it: raise prices, cut variable costs, or reduce the $60,000 of traceable costs
Qualitative: customers may buy shoes together with other FitTech gear, so closing could hurt other divisions' sales
Also consider employee morale, brand image and supplier relationships

calculations.label: Segment margin statement, Smart Shoes
steps: Sales $300,000 minus variable expenses $200,000 = contribution margin $100,000
Contribution margin $100,000 minus traceable fixed costs $60,000 = segment margin $40,000
Segment margin $40,000 minus common allocated costs $65,000 = reported net loss ($25,000)

calculations.label: Effect on company net income of dropping Smart Shoes
steps: Common allocated costs avoided: $0 (they are reassigned to the other divisions)
Change in company net income: 60,000 minus 100,000 = ($40,000)

judge_question_answers.question: If we shouldn't use net loss to evaluate the Smart Shoes division manager, what should we use?
answer: Use the segment margin (or the contribution margin together with the traceable costs the manager controls)
The manager controls sales, variable costs and traceable fixed costs, not the headquarters allocation
Judging a manager on allocated costs they cannot control is unfair and can lead to bad decisions

judge_question_answers.question: Is there any situation where dropping Smart Shoes would be the right decision?
answer: Yes, if the segment margin turned negative, meaning the division could not cover its own traceable costs
Or if the resources used by Smart Shoes (space, staff, advertising budget) could earn more than $40,000 elsewhere: that is the opportunity cost
Or if closing it would free up capacity for a more profitable product line
Even then, weigh the effect on sales of the other divisions

key_concepts.definition: A part of a business, such as a division, product line or region, for which managers want separate cost and profit information.
Sales minus variable expenses; the amount left to cover fixed costs and profit. Contribution margin = sales minus variable expenses.
A fixed cost that exists only because of a particular segment and would be eliminated if that segment were dropped.
A fixed cost that supports several segments, such as headquarters rent, and would not go away if one segment were dropped.
A segment's contribution margin minus its traceable fixed costs; the best measure of a segment's long-run profitability. Segment margin = contribution margin minus traceable fixed costs.
Assigning a share of a common cost to segments using a base such as sales or floor space; allocations do not change the total cost the company pays.
A cost that changes between two alternatives; only these costs are relevant to a keep or drop decision.
Comparing only the future revenues and costs that differ between alternatives when making a decision.
The benefit given up by choosing one alternative over another, such as the profit a freed-up resource could earn elsewhere.
Accounting information prepared for internal decision-making by managers, such as segment reports and cost analyses, rather than for outside investors.

notes: ICDC level because students must rebuild the divisional income statement in segment margin format, prove that the $25,000 loss is created by an allocation, and defend a recommendation against a determined CEO. Watch for students who treat the $65,000 as avoidable or who stop at contribution margin without subtracting traceable costs. This uses the same relevant costing logic as ACT-NEW-STATE-4 (CoreTech make or buy), so avoid assigning both to the same student in one practice session.

items.label: Describe types of costs used in managerial accounting

criteria.exceeds: Separates the $200,000 of variable expenses, the $60,000 of traceable fixed costs (shoe supervisors and shoe advertising, which disappear if the division closes) and the $65,000 of common fixed costs (headquarters rent and CEO salary, which stay), and explains that only avoidable (differential) costs matter for the drop decision.
criteria.meets: Correctly explains that the $60,000 of traceable fixed costs would go away if Smart Shoes closed, while the $65,000 of common costs would remain.
criteria.below: Defines traceable and common costs in general terms but does not apply them to the Smart Shoes amounts, or treats part of the $65,000 as avoidable.
criteria.little: Does not distinguish cost types, or treats all $125,000 of fixed costs as avoidable.

items.label: Describe marginal analysis techniques and applications

criteria.exceeds: Walks through the incremental analysis: $300,000 of revenue lost, $200,000 of variable costs and $60,000 of traceable costs saved, so company net income falls by $40,000 instead of rising by the $25,000 the CEO expects, and notes the opportunity cost of the division's resources.
criteria.meets: Shows that dropping Smart Shoes would lower company net income by $40,000 because the lost $100,000 contribution margin exceeds the $60,000 of costs saved.
criteria.below: Recognizes the CEO's $25,000 estimate is wrong but gives an incorrect effect, for example stopping at the $100,000 contribution margin.
criteria.little: Agrees that dropping the division raises profit by $25,000, or gives no analysis.

items.label: Explain the nature of managerial accounting

criteria.exceeds: Explains that segment reports are internal tools for decisions like keep or drop, rebuilds the statement as contribution margin $100,000, segment margin $40,000 and reported loss ($25,000), and shows Smart Shoes contributes $40,000 a year toward common costs and profit.
criteria.meets: Calculates a contribution margin of $100,000 and a segment margin of $40,000 and uses them to evaluate the division.
criteria.below: Calculates the contribution margin but stops without subtracting the $60,000 of traceable costs, or gets the segment margin wrong.
criteria.little: Does not calculate contribution margin or segment margin.

items.label: Discuss the nature of cost allocation

criteria.exceeds: Explains that the $65,000 is an allocation of company-wide costs that does not change total cost, so closing Smart Shoes just shifts it to the other two divisions, and that the $25,000 net loss exists only because of that allocation.
criteria.meets: States that the $65,000 of allocated costs would stay and be charged to the other divisions if Smart Shoes were dropped.
criteria.below: Mentions allocation but is unsure whether the $65,000 would go away, or does not link it to the $25,000 loss.
criteria.little: Treats the allocated costs as savings from closing the division, or ignores them.

criteria.exceeds: Delivers a well organized, persuasive presentation that respectfully challenges the CEO's plan, leads with the $40,000 finding, and closes with a clear recommendation to keep and improve Smart Shoes.
criteria.meets: Presents the cost types, segment margin, effect of dropping and recommendation in a clear, logical order.
criteria.below: Presentation is disorganized, reads from notes, or buries the key $40,000 finding.
criteria.little: Presentation is unclear, incomplete or does not reach a recommendation.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects the division's result to the whole company: the $65,000 moves to the other divisions, company profit drops $40,000, and shoe customers may stop buying other FitTech gear.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly that the reported loss is caused by an allocation and that the division adds $40,000 to company profit.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or misses how closing affects the other divisions.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Recommends keeping Smart Shoes and improving it by raising prices, cutting variable costs or reducing the $60,000 of traceable costs, and adds qualitative reasons such as bundled customer purchases, employee morale, brand image and supplier relationships.
criteria.meets: Makes a clear recommendation to keep Smart Shoes with at least one financial and one qualitative reason.
criteria.below: Gives a hesitant or partly supported recommendation, or offers no qualitative reasons.
criteria.little: Makes no recommendation, or recommends dropping the division.

criteria.exceeds: Explains contribution margin, segment margin and allocated costs in plain language the CEO can follow, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the calculations and recommendation clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a segment margin statement or simple visual that shows how $300,000 of sales becomes a $40,000 segment margin and a ($25,000) reported loss, and suggests creative ways to improve the division's margin.
criteria.meets: Organizes the segment data in a way that makes the difference between the loss and the segment margin easy to see.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: judge the manager on segment margin because the manager controls sales, variable costs and traceable costs but not the headquarters allocation; and dropping would be right only if the segment margin turned negative or the division's resources could earn more than $40,000 elsewhere, while still weighing effects on other divisions' sales.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including using segment margin to evaluate the manager and naming a negative segment margin as a reason to drop.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without reasons.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or gives incorrect answers such as judging the manager on net loss.

key_points: Traceable fixed costs ($60,000) disappear if Smart Shoes closes; common allocated costs ($65,000) stay and shift to the other divisions
Segment margin = $100,000 minus $60,000 = $40,000; the ($25,000) loss appears only after the $65,000 allocation
Dropping Smart Shoes lowers company net income by $40,000, not raises it by $25,000
Recommend keeping the division and improving it through prices, variable costs or traceable costs
Qualitative factors: customers buying shoes with other FitTech gear, employee morale, brand image and supplier relationships
Evaluate the division manager on segment margin, not net loss after allocations
